metaTitle: Best Immersion Blenders for Soup in 2026
metaDescription: Six immersion blenders for soup compared on motor power, shaft length, splash control and pot protection, from 350 to 1100 watts.
expertTake: The KOIOS 5-in-1 is the pick for most soup cooks because its 1000-watt copper motor, 12 speeds plus turbo and anti-splash stainless shaft handle thick purees without stalling. The Waring Quik Stix is the commercial pick for stockpots. Skip a stick blender if your soups are chunky, because chopping and stirring do more than blending.
introParagraphs: Soup is where an immersion blender earns its place. You blend directly in the pot, so there is no pouring hot liquid into a pitcher, no transfer losses and one fewer thing to wash.

Soup also exposes weak sticks quickly. Thick vegetable purees, dense beans and cream soups load the motor, and a short shaft or open blade turns a pot into a splatter zone. This comparison sorts the lineup on those soup-specific limits.

products.name: KOIOS 5-in-1 Hand Immersion Blender 1000W 12 Speed
products.description:
A 1000-watt copper motor and 12 speeds plus a turbo button make this the most controllable stick for soup. Start on the lowest speed to draw the soup into the blade without splashing, then step up as the vegetables break down. Turbo clears stubborn lumps at the end.

The anti-splash 304 stainless steel shaft is the reason it works well in a standard pot. The shaft is designed to keep the blade near the bottom while limiting how far liquid climbs. Against the 400-watt MasterChef, the extra reserve is obvious on cooked potatoes and squash, where cheaper motors slow and warm up.

The five-in-one kit adds a chopper, whisk, frother and beaker, which is more than most soup cooks need, but the beaker is useful for sauces. Wash the shaft by hand, keep the motor head dry and blend in bursts of a minute or two so the motor can cool. For soup specifically, it is the best balance of power and control here. Over years of use the plastic motor housing and cord are the likely wear points, not the copper windings, so coil the cord loosely and never hang the unit by it. Against the Ganiza, which offers four more speeds, the KOIOS adds a turbo button that is handy for clearing the last lumps from a thick puree.
products.bestFor: Thick vegetable and bean soups blended in a standard pot.
pros: 12 speeds plus turbo give fine control
Full kit with beaker and whisk
cons: Wattage claim is input power, not sustained output
Newer brand with a thinner support network

products.name: Waring Quik Stix Plus 10-Inch Immersion Blender 350W
products.description:
Waring builds this for commercial kitchens, and it shows in the details: a sealed stainless steel shaft, a removable 10-inch immersion arm and a variable speed motor rated at roughly half a horsepower. The sealed design means no seams for soup to creep into.

Ten inches of shaft reaches the bottom of a deep stockpot, which is the main reason to buy it for large batches. The 350-watt motor is modest next to the KOIOS at 1000 watts, but a commercial duty rating suggests better thermal management and a longer service life than a cheap 1000-watt claim.

It costs more than the consumer sticks and has a commercial feel, with fewer accessories in the box. It is the right pick for cooks who make soup in large pots weekly and want a tool that can be washed and sanitized repeatedly. In daily kitchen use, its sealed shaft cleans quickly and does not trap soup, which matters when you blend dairy-based soups. Against the KOIOS, you pay more for build and reach, not for wattage, so choose it because of the stockpot and the duty cycle.
products.bestFor: Large stockpots and frequent heavy use.

products.name: Turelar 1100W 5-in-1 Immersion Blender Nylon Guard
products.description:
The Turelar leads with an 1100-watt full copper motor and a food-grade nylon blade guard that is intended to protect non-stick and enameled pots. If your soup pot is Le Creuset-style enamel or a non-stick saucepan, a nylon guard is a real advantage over bare stainless.

The trigger gives variable speed, so you press harder to blend faster, which is easy to learn. Against the KOIOS, you lose the 12-speed range but gain a simple trigger and a pot-friendly guard. It also has a higher wattage claim, though both numbers describe input power.

Cleaning is simple with a detachable shaft. The five-in-one set adds attachments you may not use. For cooks with expensive pots and thick soups, it is a sensible choice. Against the Ganiza at 1000 watts, the Turelar claims more power but fewer speed steps, so the real choice is trigger simplicity against a dial. Remember that nylon guards can warp if left against a hot burner, so rest the stick on a plate.
products.bestFor: Enameled and non-stick pots with thick soups.
cons: Fewer speed steps than the KOIOS

products.name: Ganiza 5-in-1 Immersion Blender 1000W 16 Speeds
products.description:
Sixteen speeds on a 1000-watt pure copper motor give the widest control of the six. For soup this means a very gentle start to prevent splatter and a gradual ramp up as the vegetables soften. It also comes with an 800 mL beaker, larger than most beakers in this class.

Compared with the KOIOS's 12 speeds and turbo, the Ganiza offers four more steps but no dedicated turbo button. In practice, the difference is subtle, and both will puree a pot of vegetable soup in a minute or two. Pick based on which control layout you prefer.

Ownership notes include cleaning the beaker and attachments, which are more parts than a simple stick. For a cook who likes fine control, it is a strong option. It pairs well with a large pot of lentil or bean soup, where slow starts prevent a volcano of hot liquid. Against the Bonsenkitchen, it has twice the stated wattage and a larger beaker, so it suits bigger batches.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want very fine speed control.
cons: More attachments to wash and store

products.name: Bonsenkitchen 4-in-1 Immersion Blender 500W 20 Speeds
products.description:
The Bonsenkitchen pairs a 500-watt high-torque motor with 20 speeds and a turbo mode. That is a middle motor in this lineup, more than the Waring's 350 W and less than the 1000-watt units, with the widest speed range of all.

For soup, the broad speed dial lets you start at a crawl and build up, which minimizes splatter in a hot pot. The food processor attachment adds a small chopping bowl, handy for onion or herbs before they go into the pot.

It is a good value pick for people who want a mid-power motor and plenty of control. Treat it as a smaller-pot tool and blend thick soups in batches. The extra speeds make a visible difference when you are blending cream soups that foam if started too fast. Against the MasterChef it costs more, but it gives you meaningful reserve and control that thin-soup sticks cannot match.
products.bestFor: Mid-size pots and cooks who want a broad speed dial.

products.name: MasterChef Immersion Blender 400W Stainless Steel
products.description:
The MasterChef is the lowest-cost stick here, with a 400-watt motor and a stainless steel blending arm. It handles light soups, tomato bisque and batters, and the stainless arm resists stains and odors.

Against the KOIOS and Ganiza, it has less than half the wattage claim and fewer speeds. That means thick potato or squash soups will take longer and may need two rounds. It also has no beaker or chopper, which keeps the price down.

It is a straightforward stick for occasional soup. Keep the blade submerged, blend in short bursts and let the motor rest. It makes sense as a first stick or a spare for the camp kitchen, and a poor sense as a daily driver for thick soups. Against the Waring, it trades commercial reach and sealed build for a much lower cost.
products.bestFor: Occasional light soups at the lowest cost.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Cooked potatoes, squash and beans are the toughest soup loads. A 1000-watt copper motor, as in the KOIOS and Ganiza, purees them without bogging down, while the 350-watt Waring and 400-watt MasterChef take more time. Wattage is input power, so judge by sustained use and let the motor rest between bursts. A good habit is to blend in two passes: coarse first, then fine, to avoid stalling the motor.

A stockpot 10 inches deep needs a long shaft, and the Waring's 10-inch arm is the longest here. Short shafts force you to tilt the pot or blend in smaller batches. Measure your deepest pot before you buy.

Hot soup splashes when the blade breaks the surface. The KOIOS anti-splash shaft, the Turelar nylon guard and the Waring sealed shaft all help. Start slow, keep the blade submerged and tilt the pot slightly. Fill the pot no more than two thirds, because soup climbs the shaft as it moves.
A bare steel blade can scratch non-stick and enameled pots. The Turelar nylon guard protects them, while stainless shafts require care. Choose based on your cookware.

More speeds mean gentler starts. The Ganiza has 16, the Bonsenkitchen has 20 plus turbo and the KOIOS has 12 plus turbo, while the MasterChef has simpler settings. A slow start is more useful than a high top speed. Foaming cream soups benefit most from a slow start.
Do not lift the blade out of hot soup while running. Fill the pot no more than two thirds, and keep the motor housing above the liquid. A removable shaft makes cleaning safer.

faq.q: Is an immersion blender safe for hot soup?
faq.a: Yes, in the pot. Keep the blade submerged, tilt the pot slightly and blend in short bursts. Do not lift the blade out while running. Let very hot soup cool for a few minutes first, because splatter burns are the usual injury.

faq.q: How much power do I need for soup?
faq.a: 350 to 500 watts handles thin soups. For thick purees, 1000 watts, as in the KOIOS and Ganiza, runs smoother. Cooking the vegetables until very soft also reduces the load on any motor.
A bare steel blade can. Use a nylon guard like the Turelar's or a pan guard. Resting the stick on a plate afterward also keeps soup off the counter.

faq.q: Immersion blender or countertop blender for soup?
faq.a: The immersion blender is easier because you blend in the pot. A countertop blender gives a smoother texture but requires pouring hot liquid, which is riskier.
Yes, partially. Blend a portion of the pot and leave the rest chunky for texture.
Many are, but check the manual. Hand washing protects the blade.
